description: Californium is a synthetic actinide element with symbol Cf and atomic number 98, first synthesized in 1950 at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory by bombarding curium with alpha particles. It is a silvery-white metal that is the sixth transuranium element to be synthesized and has the second-highest atomic mass of all elements produced in visible quantities.
uses: Californium has practical applications as a neutron source, including helping to start up nuclear reactors, studying materials through neutron diffraction and neutron spectroscopy, treating certain cervical and brain cancers, conducting neutron activation analysis, and synthesizing higher mass elements. Certain isotopes of californium, particularly 252Cf, are used for these purposes because they emit neutrons.
characteristics: Californium is a malleable metal with a melting point of 900 ± 30 °C and an estimated boiling point of 1,743 K. It exhibits oxidation states of 4, 3, or 2, with the +3 state being dominant, and slowly tarnishes in air at room temperature. The element has two crystalline forms at standard pressure: an alpha form below 600–800 °C with density of 15.10 g/cm3 and a beta form above 600–800 °C with density of 8.74 g/cm3.
